blocks.text: When you mark a column as PII, Omnisient ensures it is anonymized and tokenized before upload, so your sensitive data is protected from the start. We use SMPC (Secure Multi-Party Computation) to keep these fields private while still enabling secure linking and collaboration across datasets. This approach helps support compliance with regulations such as POPIA, GDPR, and UAE data protection laws.
Summary of Supported Fields

Helps verify payments or reconcile transactions while keeping the full card number protected.
A full payment card number used for secure matching or transaction linking when required.

Supports person-level matching across datasets using a commonly available identifier.
Must follow standard email formats (e.g., name@domain.com).
Helps support name-based matching for use cases where names are needed (often alongside surname).
Used for healthcare / insurance matching and analysis while protecting member identity.
Enables secure transaction analysis and matching for retailers, payment providers, and financial institutions.
Used when matching individuals who do not have a national ID in the dataset.
Allows tokenized tracking of payment accounts (e.g., customer account references) across datasets.
Common identifier for matching customer records when email/ID is unavailable.

blocks.text: Formatting Guidelines
Quick formatting guide
Omnisient automatically applies formatting adjustments (such as trimming spaces, standardizing case, or removing special characters where relevant) to every dataset before validation.
Tip: To ensure a smoother upload, we encourage formatting your source data close to the expected shape where feasible.

rows:
- Trim spaces
- Remove spaces & special characters
- Letters, accents, spaces, hyphens, apostrophes supported

- 13 digits
- Numeric only
- First 6 digits represent a valid date

- No enforced format
- Avoid mixed identifiers in one column

- Trim spaces
- Use a consistent format

- International numbers start with +
- Local numbers may start with 0 or without
- Should be a length of 17 characters

blocks.text: Social Security Number
An SSN consists of 9 digits, commonly displayed in the following format:

rows: Area Number (first 3 digits). Historically linked to geography, but no longer reflects location.
Group Number (next 2 digits). Used for administrative sequencing.
Serial Number (last 4 digits). Sequential within each group.

blocks.text: Your validation checks

headers: Examples of invalid and valid formats
rows: SSN must contain exactly 9 digits (excluding optional dashes).
Only numeric characters are allowed (dashes are optional).
Letters or special characters are invalid
No section may be entirely zero.
Known placeholder or example values are rejected.

Repeating or sequential digits is invalid:
123-45-6789
111-11-1111
SSN must follow the AAA-GG-SSSS structure.
Incorrect length or malformed values are invalid

blocks.text: South African Company Business Registration Number
The platform automatically validates two formats for South African company registration numbers:
Post-2002 CIPC Format Validation
Expected Pattern
YYYY/NNNNNN/NN

items: YYYY = year (2008 → current year)
NNNNNN = exactly 6 digits
NN = 2-digit entity type (e.g., 07 = Private Company)

blocks.text: Your validation checks

items: Regex must match the pattern
First 4 characters must be numeric (year)
Year must be no later than the current year
Input must contain exactly two slashes
All other characters must be digits

blocks.text: Old / Regional Format Validation
Expected Pattern
XYYYY/NNNNNN

items: X = a single alphabetic region code
YYYY = year (no later than the current year)
NNNNNN = 6 digits

blocks.text: Your validation checks

items: Regex must match the old/regional pattern
First character must be a letter
Next 4 must form a valid year
Input must contain one slash
All remaining characters (after the first letter) must be digits or a slash

blocks.text: If a record does not conform to either format, it will be flagged during the transformation step for further review.

chapters.title: Jupyter Notebook
chapters.part: Analytics tools: SQLPad, Jupyter and Power BI

blocks.text: Python, a widely used programming language for data scientists, offers a wide selection of libraries that you can install with the pip command, simplifying complex calculations and data analysis tasks. It also facilitates the automation of tasks and processes, streamlining workflows for enhanced productivity and efficiency.

is an open-source web application that's become one of the go-to tools for data scientists, analysts, and even educators in recent years. It provides an environment where you can write live code, equations, visualizations, and narrative text - all in a single document, making it a versatile choice for a variety of data projects.

What sets Jupyter Notebook apart is its ability to combine code execution with data visualization and rich text, facilitating a more interactive and insightful data exploration process. You can jot down your thought process while simultaneously running code snippets, making it an excellent tool for both the development and sharing of data analyses.
Getting started
Two things must be in place before you can access Jupyter Notebook in Omnisient:

items: An active Jupyter Notebook subscription - your organization must have Jupyter Notebook enabled as part of your plan.
A compatible project type - the project you are working in must have analytical tools enabled.

blocks.text: If Jupyter Notebook is not showing in your project, it is likely one of these two reasons.
You can access Jupyter Notebook from two places:

rows: Open your project and select Open With > Jupyter Notebook.
Available via the Datasets and the project sections in the side navigation.

blocks.text: Each user has their own isolated Jupyter environment, you won't see other users' notebooks or files, and your workspace can be configured to suit your needs.

Having trouble loading Jupyter?
- Refresh the page and try again.
- Check your project status - Jupyter will not load if the project is in a Processing or Failed state.
- Log out and log back in to refresh your session.
- Check with your IT team that all required URLs and IP ranges are whitelisted. See Firewall Access Required for details.
Workspace size options
Three workspace sizes are available, allowing you to match compute resources to the demands of your work:
Resources in Omnisient's AKS environment are allocated dynamically and managed by Kubernetes, which ensures efficient utilization of available resources while maintaining performance and scalability.

items: Resource limits and requests - each project is allocated resources based on predefined minimum and maximum limits. The minimum (resource request) ensures each Jupyter instance has enough resources to start and run. The maximum (resource limit) prevents any single instance from consuming excessive resources, ensuring fair distribution across all users.

Pod initialization - when a user opens a Jupyter instance, Kubernetes uses the defined resource requests and limits to create a new instance, known as a pod. A pod is a virtual environment that encapsulates the Jupyter application and its dependencies.

Scaling mechanism -the AKS setup includes a single server and two scale set instances to handle varying workloads. When resource usage reaches a threshold, Kubernetes automatically provisions additional instances. When demand decreases, it scales down and frees up resources.
Virtual server fit - each pod fits within the size constraints of the virtual server in use. Kubernetes continuously monitors resource usage and adjusts allocation to optimize performance.

Resource monitoring and management - Kubernetes provides built-in mechanisms for monitoring usage and managing pod lifecycle, ensuring each Jupyter instance operates within defined resource limits without impacting overall system performance.

blocks.text: File browser

When you launch Jupyter in a project, the left panel opens by default to the File Browser. This displays your persisted storage - files, notebooks, and code saved here are maintained between Jupyter sessions, so your work is preserved each time you return to the project.
From the file browser you can:

items: Create a new launcher - add a new .ipynb notebook, text file, .py file, and more
Upload a file from your local computer to your project
Create a folder within your file browser space

blocks.text: You can also write files out from your notebook directly to the file browser. Files are written to the project rather than to your local disk. For example, a dataframe can be written out as a .csv using standard Pandas functionality:
In a later session, you can read the file back into memory:
Any file that can be created using Python scripting can be written and stored in persisted storage.
Right-click context menu
Right-clicking a file in the file browser reveals additional options. Most of these are standard Jupyter actions - Open, Rename, Delete, Cut, Copy, and so on. One option is specific to Omnisient:
- submits a notebook for review and inclusion in your organization's Company Notebook Library. See Company Notebook Library below.
Working with your data in Jupyter

reads data from the data warehouse into a Jupyter notebook, either from your own Data Preparation area or a project's shared tables. Queries are written as SQL strings and submitted through the omni_hub magic command; the result is a ResultSet object you convert to a pandas DataFrame with .DataFrame().
Viewing available tables
Before querying, load the extension and list the tables available to you:

items: Load the extension:

blocks.text: %load_ext omni_hub

items: Return every table in a project:

blocks.text: %omni_hub --list-tables
Querying data
Define the query as a SQL string, submit it through omni_hub, then convert the result to a DataFrame:

%load_ext omni_hub
data = %omni_hub {'select top 100 * from [project_code].[table_name]'}
df = data.DataFrame()
print(df)

items: Replace [project_code] with the project code, for example ClientName_Prj_00001. For Own Data Preparation, use ClientName_a.
Replace [table_name] with the table to query.
top 100 limits the extract to the first 100 rows. Remove it to pull the full table.

blocks.text: Queries use Microsoft SQL Server syntax, and can join a table against a partner's table within the same query – join on DW_ID_KEY or BestMatchID.
To identify a username for support queries or table-creation permission requests:
%omni_hub {'select current_user'}
The username is the long alphanumeric string ending in the project name.

Tips for managing memory:
- For large datasets, do as much data preparation, cleaning, joining, and sampling in SQL as possible before loading into the notebook – Python compute may run out of memory on very large datasets.
- Load only the data needed – a filtered query over a full table pull.
- Clear unused variables with Python's del, or restart the kernel to free memory between tasks.
Choosing a workspace size for a query
Query performance and processing time depend on the shape of the table being pulled, and the notebook's workspace size needs to match it.

items: A wide table (many columns, e.g. 500 columns across 3 million rows) is compute- and memory-intensive to process column-by-column, and typically needs the Extra Large workspace size.
A long table (few columns, e.g. 10 columns across 50 million rows) processes differently – the Large workspace size is typically sufficient.

blocks.text: See Workspace size options above for the full CPU/memory breakdown of each workspace size.

Pulling more data than a query actually needs increases the risk of the query timing out, independent of workspace size. Scope a query to the columns and rows actually needed rather than sizing up to compensate.
Optimizing memory for large tables

omni_hub returns a ResultSet object. Converting it directly to a DataFrame holds the data twice in memory – once as the ResultSet, once as the DataFrame – which can cause out-of-memory errors on large tables.
Export the ResultSet to CSV, delete it, then load the CSV into pandas instead. This holds only one copy at a time:

items: Run the query with omni_hub.
Save the result to CSV with .csv("path").
Delete the original object with del.
Load the CSV into pandas with pd.read_csv.

blocks.text:
# 1) Run query via omni_hub
sql_query = "select top 10 * from [project_code].[table_name]"
rs = %omni_hub {sql_query}
df = rs.DataFrame()
print(df)
df.to_csv("my_table.csv", index=False)
# 2) Save to CSV
rs.csv("my_table.csv")
# 3) Delete the ResultSet to free memory
del rs
# 4) Read the CSV into pandas
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("my_table.csv", low_memory=False)
Writing a DataFrame back to a project
To write the results of an analysis back to the project tables, use omni_lab.

items: Import the package:

blocks.text: import omni_lab

items: Copy the DataFrame back to the project:

blocks.text: omni_lab.copy_to_project_tables(df, "PROJECT_CODE", "table_name")

items: Replace PROJECT_CODE with your project code, for example QACOMPANYA_PRJ_00023, and table_name with a name of your choosing. Table names can't contain spaces.

blocks.text: The write runs asynchronously.
Libraries
Import a library using standard Python syntax:

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
To view all libraries installed on the platform, run:
!pip list
This returns an alphabetized list of all available libraries.
For the full list of packages and libraries available in Omnisient's Jupyter environment, see Available Packages & Libraries for Jupyter Notebook.
Virtual environments

A virtual environment (venv) is a persistent, isolated Python environment within a Jupyter project, separate from the project's shared Python installation. Packages installed inside a venv persist across sessions in the project's storage, avoiding the session-only installs and version drift that come with installing packages directly in the shared environment.

A venv is useful whenever a specific analysis or model needs a particular library version - for example, testing a newer release of a package without changing the version every other notebook in the project relies on. It also makes an analysis reproducible: recreating the same venv gives the same package versions, rather than whatever happens to be installed in the shared environment at the time.
Jupyter Notebook creates and activates project-specific venvs through the omni_helper extension.
Creating and activating a Venv
Run these two cells at the top of the notebook, every session:

items: Load the omni_helper extension:

blocks.text: %load_ext omni_helper

items: Create and activate the venv: Replace <env_name> with any name you choose. The first time, this creates the venv and activates it; every time after, it just activates it.

blocks.text: %omni_helper venv-activate <env_name>

Initial creation takes 15 to 30 minutes. The venv itself persists in the project's storage, but a new session still needs to run both cells (%load_ext omni_helper and %omni_helper venv-activate venv) to reactivate it - reactivating an existing venv takes seconds.
Use the same venv name across every notebook in the project, so each one activates the same persisted venv and the packages already installed in it.
Installing packages inside a Venv
Once a venv is active, install a package the same way as outside one:
!pip install <package_name>

Packages install from Omnisient's vetted package library. A package installed inside an active venv persists across sessions in the project's storage - install it once, and it's available every time that venv is reactivated, without installing it again.
See Using Jupyter Notebook for Packages/Libraries Management for how package installs behave outside a venv.
If a package isn't part of the vetted library, it isn't available to install this way. Contact support@omnisient.com to request it be added or updated.
Company Notebook Library

The Company Notebook Library allows analysts to share approved notebooks across your organization. Once a notebook has been reviewed and approved by the Omnisient team, it becomes available to all users within the company and can be copied into any project.
Accessing the library
The Notebook Library panel is available in the left sidebar within Jupyter. It displays all notebooks your organization has had approved.
To use a notebook, right-click it and select Copy into Project - a copy is added to your current project's file browser.
Promoting a notebook to the library
Any analyst can submit a notebook for inclusion in the Company Notebook Library.

Clear your notebook outputs before submitting. Notebooks submitted with outputs will be declined. Before promoting, clear all outputs - go to Edit > Clear All Outputs, or Kernel > Restart Kernel and Clear All Outputs.
To submit a notebook:

items: In the file browser, right-click the notebook you want to promote.
Select Promote to Library.
A confirmation modal appears - review and confirm your submission.
Your submission has been logged, and the Omnisient team has been notified to begin the review process.

blocks.text: What happens next
Once submitted, your notebook enters a review queue. The Omnisient team will review it and communicate the outcome by email.

items: Approved - the notebook is added to your organization's library and becomes visible to all users in the Notebook Library panel.
Declined - you will receive an email with the reason for the decline. Review the feedback, make the necessary changes, and resubmit.

blocks.text: Sharing a notebook with a project member
To share directly with a specific project member, use omni_helper.
Active participant in the project.
Jupyter Notebook open within your project.
Step 1: Load the extension
%load_ext omni_helper
Step 2: Get the recipient's user address
Run omni_helper project-members to return a list of project members and their user addresses. Copy the User Address of the intended recipient.
User addresses are project-specific - the same user has a different address in each project they belong to.
Step 3: Send the file
omni_helper send-files --paths [filename.ipynb] --receiver [user_address]
Filenames cannot contain spaces. Rename the file before transferring if needed.
Step 4: Check transfer status
Run omni_helper transfer-history and match the output against the REQUEST_ID returned when you submitted.
The file appears in a shared folder within their Jupyter workspace inside a dated subfolder. There is no automatic notification - they will need to check manually.

rows: Not an active participant in this project
Confirm they have been added to the project
Address copied from a different project
Re-run omni_helper project-members in this project

chapters.title: Using Jupyter Notebook for Package Management
chapters.part: Analytics tools: SQLPad, Jupyter and Power BI

blocks.text: Starting 30 September 2024, you will now be able to install your own packages/libraries for use in Jupyter Notebook, and the platform will no longer pre-install the packages on your behalf. This allows for faster integrations with the exact libraries and versions you wish to work with.
NOTE:
The installs do not persist across your different notebooks and will have to be run in a block at the beginning of the notebook.
How to Install Packages in Jupyter Notebook using PIP

Jupyter Notebook allows you to install and manage Python packages efficiently using PIP. This can speed up integrations and empower users with self-service capabilities. You can even install specific versions of libraries to ensure compatibility with your projects.
Step-by-step Guide

items: Open your Jupyter Notebook:
Launch Jupyter Notebook from the Omnisient web app
Insert a new code cell:
Click on a new cell or press B to create a new code block.
Install a package using PIP:
In the code cell, type the following command to install any package:

blocks.text: !pip install <package_name>

items: For example, to install the pandas package, use:

blocks.text: !pip install pandas

items: Install a specific version of a package:
If you want to install a particular version of a package, specify the version number in your command. For example:

blocks.text: !pip install pandas==1.3.3

items: Run the cell:
Press Shift + Enter to execute the command and install the package.
Jupyter will display the installation progress in the output below the code cell.
Verify the installation:
You can verify that the package was installed successfully by importing it into a new cell:

blocks.text: import pandas as pd
Available Libraries
See a full list of available libraries and packages.
Best Practices

items: Check package compatibility: Before installing, make sure the package version is compatible with your environment or other libraries you are using.

blocks.text: Troubleshooting

items: Permission denied error: If you encounter a permission issue, try adding the --user flag to your command:

blocks.text: !pip install --user <package_name>

items: Package not found: If PIP is unable to find the package, make sure that the package name is spelled correctly, or that it exists in the Python Package Index (PyPI).

blocks.text: By following these steps, you can quickly install and manage the libraries you need for your projects, empowering faster integrations and more flexible, self-service development workflows.

chapters.title: How to Create a SQLPad Export
chapters.part: Analytics tools: SQLPad, Jupyter and Power BI

blocks.text:
As part of our ongoing effort to help clients get the most out of their data collaborations, the Omnisient platform allows users to request SQLPad exports when they need to run further analysis or generate insights outside the platform. SQLPad exports provide a secure way to extract aggregated query results so you can continue your analysis in external tools, while ensuring all data shared through the export follows the same approval and security standards that apply across the platform.
The process is simple, secure, and designed to ensure that all exports go through the necessary partner and internal reviews before becoming available for download. Here’s how to create a SQLPad export.
Step 1: Navigate to the Project

Start by opening the project from which you want to create an export.
Click Open with, then select SQLPad.
Project types that currently support SQLPad exports include:

items: ACE
Overlap
Predictive Modelling on Retail Data
Financial Inclusion

blocks.text: Step 2: Build and Run Your Query

Use SQLPad to build and run your query as usual.
Once the query completes successfully, a download icon will appear (only for supported project types). Select the icon and then choose Request CSV when you are satisfied with the results you want to export.
Step 3: Submit Your SQLPad Export Request
After selecting Request CSV, a modal will open prompting you to provide a few details.
Note: This request is sent to your collaboration partners for approval, followed by an additional security check by Omnisient. Once fully approved, your export will be available for download.

rows: A random sample of rows from your export will be shared with approvers to give them context and help them assess your request.

You must confirm that Omnisient permits only the download of aggregated results.
By selecting this option, you acknowledge that your export does not contain information that could lead to the identification of any individual.
Confirm that you’ve read and agree to Omnisient’s Terms and Conditions.

blocks.text: Once everything is complete and compliant, click Request Export to submit your request.
Step 4: Monitor Your Export’s Progress

You can track the status of all your SQLPad exports under the All Files section in the side navigation. Each export follows a clear lifecycle, and its current status will tell you exactly where it is in the process.
Note: Only exports you have created will surface here.
Statues to expect and what they mean:

rows: The export has been received and Omnisient is performing additional automated security checks.

Your collaboration partners are reviewing your export.
The Approvals column shows how many partners have approved so far.
Your export has passed all reviews and is ready for download.

A collaborator has rejected your export.
You’ll receive an email with the rejection reason so you can adjust and resubmit if needed.

The export did not pass Omnisient’s security checks.
An email will explain what failed and why.
The export has expired or the underlying project has locked (for example, due to a dataset share expiry).

blocks.text: And that’s it!

You’ve successfully created a SQLPad export.
This process ensures secure, transparent collaboration while enabling you to extract valuable insights from your projects.

chapters.title: SQLPad Troubleshooting Guide
chapters.part: Analytics tools: SQLPad, Jupyter and Power BI

blocks.text: Overview
SQLPad is the SQL query editor available from Own Data Prep or inside your Omnisient project. This guide covers the most common errors users encounter and how to resolve them.
SQLPad connects directly to your project's data environment. Most errors are caused by connection timeouts, write-back errors, or session issues - not problems with your data.
How to Access SQLPad
SQLPad is accessed from Own Data Prep or inside a project:

items: Open your project from the Projects Dashboard
In the project detail view, locate the Open with option
Select SQLPad from the menu

blocks.text: If you don't see the Open with option, scroll down on the project detail page — it may be below the fold. Your project must also be in a Ready state before SQLPad can be opened.
Navigating Back to Your Project
To return to your project from SQLPad, use the breadcrumb navigation at the top of the page. Click your project name in the breadcrumb trail to go back to the project detail view.
Common Errors and Fixes
1. Error When Writing a Dataframe to SQL
You run a write operation from Jupyter (e.g., writing a dataframe back to a SQL table) and receive an error.
Confirm the exact source table name - even a small difference will cause this error. Cross-check the table name against what appears in your dataset on the Datasets page.
If the table name is correct and the error persists, contact support with:

items: Your project name
The source table name you were writing to
The full error message

blocks.text: 2. SQL Server Timeouts
Queries run for a long time and then time out, or SQLPad becomes unresponsive.
Steps to fix:

items: Add a LIMIT clause to reduce your result set — start with LIMIT 1000
Avoid SELECT * on large tables — select only the columns you need
Add filters to narrow the dataset before running aggregations
If timeouts persist on simple queries, contact support — the issue may be server-side

blocks.text: If timeouts started suddenly and your query hasn't changed, log a support ticket so the team can check server status.
3. SQLPad Fails to Load / Connection Error
SQLPad opens but shows a connection error, blank screen, or spins indefinitely.
Steps to fix:

items: Refresh the page and try opening SQLPad again
Check your project status - if it shows Processing or Failed, SQLPad will not connect until the project is ready
Log out and log back in to refresh your session
Check with your IT team that all required URLs and IP ranges are whitelisted and are not being blocked by your firewall. View Firewall Access Required for more details.

blocks.text: 4. Query Returns No Results
Query runs successfully but returns 0 rows.
Steps to fix:

items: Remove all filters and run SELECT COUNT(*) FROM [table_name] to confirm the table has data
Check that your project is using the correct dataset version - if the dataset was re-uploaded, you may be querying an older version
Check for date filters in your query - the data range may not match what is in the dataset

blocks.text: Still Stuck
Contact support with the following information - this helps the team diagnose faster:

items: Your project name
The full error message (screenshot if possible)
The query or operation you were running
The table name you were querying or writing to

blocks.text: Approvals is where you control what partners can do with your shared data. When a partner creates a project or a SQLPad export using your dataset, the request goes to Approvals, where an Admin decides whether it's allowed to proceed.

Permissions
Only users with Admin permissions can access Approvals. See the User Management article.
Where to find Approvals
In the Omnisient Platform, go to Admin → Approvals. This is your central hub for reviewing every request.
You'll get an email notification when a new request comes in, with a direct link to review it.
If a request isn't actioned in time, it will lock and the partner will be blocked.
blocks.bold_lead: Make sure to action requests as promptly.

blocks.text: Approval request types

rows: Projects a partner creates using your shared dataset

- ACE

- Financial Inclusion
SQLPad exports a partner creates from a project using your dataset
You (data owner) and an internal Omnisient reviewer

blocks.text: Project approval

Approving projects created on your data gives you control, visibility, and peace of mind around how your data is being used. This process is designed to be simple and transparent, so you always stay in the loop.
Request statuses

rows: The dataset share behind the request has expired, or the subscription has expired.

blocks.text: How to review

items: Find the request and click Review in the final column.
Check the request details in the modal that opens. The review shows the request details, along with the shared dataset that the partner wants to use to create the project.
Click Approve or Reject.

rows: The requestor gets a confirmation email and the request moves into processing.
A modal opens asking for a rejection reason. Be specific here. It appears in the requestor's rejection email, so a clear reason means they know exactly what to fix before resubmitting their request.

blocks.text: The review modal breaks the request into two sections:

rows: The name of the partner, the project type, date of request and project code.
The shared dataset's name, dates, status, and who shared it.

blocks.text: SQLPad export request approval

Approving SQLPad exports is an important part of ensuring that your data is used responsibly and transparently. It gives you clear visibility into how your data contributes to insights, while keeping you in control of what gets exported.
Once a SQLPad export is approved, Omnisient can no longer track or control copies saved locally by the user.
Request statuses
How to review

items: Find the request and click Review in the final column.
Check the request details in the modal that opens.
Click Approve or Reject.

rows: This will now be followed by an additional security check by Omnisient.
A modal opens asking for a rejection reason. Be specific here. It appears in the requestor's rejection email, so a clear reason means they know exactly what to fix before resubmitting their request.

blocks.text: The review modal breaks the request into six sections:

rows: Overview of what the export contains.
Unique identifier linking the export to its originating project - reference this if you contact support.
The dataset used to generate the export.
A preview of rows and columns, so you can judge whether you're comfortable with what's being shared. Unsure how to read it? See the Up-Skilling Guide: How to Assess SQLPad Exports with Confidence.
Record count once approved, plus a reminder that exports expire 14 days after approval.
A prompt to confirm you acknowledge and agree to Omnisient's data usage terms governing SQLPad approvals.

chapters.title: Up-Skilling Guide: How to Assess SQLPad Exports with Confidence
chapters.part: Analytics tools: SQLPad, Jupyter and Power BI

blocks.text: As part of our ongoing effort to help clients get the most out of the data collaboration and enhancement capabilities that the Omnisient platform provides we've added SQLPad exports as a way to support insight generation and data analysis.

Protecting customer data sits at the core of everything that we do and our SQLPad export process is designed so that PII never leaves the system, and that export results are strictly limited to non-PII fields, with multiple guardrails in place to support this.

The review and approval process adds a critical human validation layer, giving you final control over how your data generates value in the marketplace. Your approval controls what insights leave your datasets while protecting your data assets and customer privacy.
This guide provides objective criteria to help you approve confidently while protecting your data assets.
The Golden Rule
If you're unsure about any aspect of an export request: Reject for clarification.
Rejecting an export is not always a denial, it's a request for more information. The data buyer can revise their query or our support team can assist.
It is always safer to reject and clarify than to approve something you don't fully understand.
This protects both you and the data buyer: you maintain control over your data asset and they receive only compliant data exports that they can confidently use.
Understanding What You're Reviewing
What the Platform Already Blocks (You Won't See These)
These are automatically restricted and cannot appear in export requests:

rows: Information that can directly identify an individual, such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, or government-issued identifiers. PII is never allowed to leave the platform.

Data that has been transformed into a fixed-length string using a mathematical process. Hashing is often used to protect sensitive values, but hashed data can still behave like an identifier and is therefore restricted.

blocks.text: What You're Reviewing (Allowed if Appropriate)

rows: A method of summarising data (for example, counts or averages) rather than showing individual records.
Information that does not directly identify an individual. SQLPad exports are limited to non-PII fields.

blocks.text: Red Flags to Watch For (Obfuscation Techniques)

rows: The practice of renaming a column when preparing data for export. This is commonly done to make data easier to read, but it can also make it less clear what the original field represents if the name is very generic or unexpected.
A value used to distinguish or reference a specific record, such as a key or reference number. Identifiers are often consistent in format and may appear sequential or structured.
A system-generated key used to link data across internal tables. SKEY values are not visible within SQLPad but may appear as references in exports under certain conditions.
A data warehouse key used internally to reference records. DW keys are identifiers and are restricted from being exported directly.

blocks.text:
Your Job
Verify that what buyers are requesting matches the category they claim, and watch for attempts to disguise restricted data as allowed data.
Awareness Tips for Reviewing Export Samples

While SQLPad exports has been designed with strong safeguards to prevent sensitive information from ever being exported, it’s still helpful to build familiarity with how data may appear in different formats. Occasionally, values might be presented in ways that are unexpected or unfamiliar, simply because of how users structure their queries or label their columns.

By understanding these patterns, you’ll feel more confident when reviewing a sample and recognizing when something may need a second look or clarification. This section highlights a few indicators that may prompt you to pause and double-check.
1. Column Names and Labels

Column names provide the first layer of context when reviewing a dataset. In most cases, they clearly describe the information being shared. It can be helpful to pause and ensure the names align with the dataset and its intended purpose.
Things to consider:

items: Do the column names make sense for this dataset? For example, would it be reasonable for a demographics export to include a column related to revenue or transactions?
Are any column names very generic (e.g. value, info, result) and therefore unclear about what they represent?
Do any column names reference inherently sensitive concepts (such as salary or credit-related terms) that might benefit from additional context?
Are there minor spelling variations or typos that make the meaning less clear?

blocks.text: Clear and well-aligned naming generally makes review easier. If a name feels unclear, a quick clarification can help ensure shared understanding.
2. How the Data Behaves
Beyond the column name, the values themselves can provide useful context. Looking at how data behaves across rows often helps confirm whether it aligns with what the label suggests.
Things to consider:

items: Do the values vary in a way you would normally expect for this type of data?
Are numbers unusually consistent, sequential, or uniformly structured?
Do text values appear to follow a fixed pattern or length across all rows?

blocks.text: 3. Formatting and Presentation
Formatting choices can sometimes make data easier to read and sometimes make it harder to interpret at a glance.
Things to consider:

items: Are currency symbols, prefixes, or units applied consistently?
Do decimals, number formats, or text styles align with what you would expect?
Are there mixed formats within the same column (e.g. numbers and text together)?

blocks.text: If formatting makes a column harder to interpret, it’s reasonable to pause and ask for clarification.
4. Dataset Context and Intended Use
Stepping back and considering the dataset as a whole can be one of the most helpful review techniques.
Things to consider:

items: Does the sample feel consistent with the type of information being shared?
Does it align with what the data partner requested and would reasonably need?
Would the dataset still make sense if one or two column names were changed?

blocks.text: This broader context check often helps confirm whether everything fits together as expected.
Examples: What to Approve vs. Reject
Scenario 1: Rejected - Disguised Identifiers
A financial services company requests "customer segmentation data" for marketing purposes.
Why This Fails

rows: Generic and vague. "value_bracket" and "activity_score" don't clearly describe what they measure.
Sequential numbering in "customer_type" (10001, 10002, 10003, 10004) suggests individual identifiers.
Each row appears unique, this suggests data that's not truly aggregated.
Column aliasing hides the true meaning. "value_bracket" could be income and "activity_score" could be a customer ID.

blocks.text: Reviewer Decision: Reject

"This export contains sequential identifiers (PREM_10001, 10002...) rather than aggregated segments. Please revise to show true customer categories (e.g., 'Premium Customers', 'Standard Customers') with counts or percentages rather than individual customer records."
Scenario 2: Rejected - Highly Granular Aggregations
A retailer requests "aggregated shopping behavior insights" across multiple dimensions.
Why This Fails

rows: Five dimensions combined create micro-segments of 1-3 customers each.
Highly specific combinations could identify individuals e.g., "23-24 year old in Sandton earning 45-47K buying luxury beauty in March".
Claims to be "aggregated" but group sizes are so small they're essentially individual records.
Combined attributes create unique or near-unique fingerprints.

blocks.text: Reviewer Decision: Reject

"This aggregation is too granular, creating segments of 1-3 customers that could enable re-identification. Please reduce dimensions (e.g., broader age groups: '20-30', larger geographic areas: 'Northern Suburbs') or focus on fewer combined attributes to ensure meaningful group sizes of 10+ customers."
Scenario 3: Rejected - Mismatched Columns and Values
A telecommunications company requests "customer demographic insights" for market research.
Why This Fails

rows: "customer_segment" shows sequential numbers instead of meaningful categories.
Numbers 8847392, 8847396 etc. appear to be system-generated customer IDs.
"customer_segment" suggests categorical segments but contains numerical identifiers.
Sequential numbering is a clear red flag for individual identifiers

blocks.text: Reviewer Decision: Reject

"The 'customer_segment' column contains sequential numerical values (8847392, 8847393...) that appear to be customer identifiers rather than segment names. Please replace with descriptive segment labels like 'High Value', 'Regular User', 'Occasional Customer' etc."
Scenario 4: Approved - Proper Aggregated Insights
A bank requests customer behavior analysis for product development and marketing strategy.
Why This Passes

rows: All columns clearly describe what they measure: age_group, account_type, etc.
Age ranges are broad (7-14 year spans), spending in ranges, not exact amounts.
Customer counts range from 445-2,156 - true aggregation with substantial group sizes
No sequential numbering or unique values that could identify individuals.
Account types and frequency bands use descriptive labels.
Data aligns with data-buyers purpose of product development.

blocks.text: Reviewer Decision: Approved
This export demonstrates proper aggregation with meaningful customer segments, appropriate group sizes, and clear business utility without privacy risks.
A Quick Review Checklist to Guide Your Decision

Before approving an export, verify all of the following criteria is met. If any of the criteria fails reject for clarification. If you are unsure that the criteria has passed reject for clarification.

rows: All column names clearly describe the data.
Columns do not reference restricted concepts.
There is no obvious obfuscation through naming.
Misspellings or very generic labels that could hide identifiers.
The values match what column names suggest.
The data varies naturally, not in suspicious patterns.
Sequential numbers (1,2,3,4) or uniform formats (AAAA1234, AAAA1235)
No high-cardinality in supposedly aggregated fields.
"Customer_Segment" column has unique values across all rows
Claims "aggregated insights" but every row is unique.
Nothing feels inconsistent with previous approved exports from this buyer.
Could these fields be combined with other data to re-identify individuals?
If YES → Reject or escalate for expert review.
Would you be comfortable explaining this approval in a compliance audit?

blocks.text: Support & Escalation

If you need support or feel unsure about an export, don’t hesitate to reach out to the support team. The requester’s email is included in the export, so you may also contact them directly if you’d like additional clarity or context.
Reject an export directly if:

items: The issue is clear (disguised identifiers, mismatched columns, vague naming).
Your rejection reason can guide the buyer to fix it.
This is a standard case covered by the guide.

blocks.text: Escalate to support if:

items: You suspect intentional policy violation or repeated problematic requests from the same buyer.
Technical question about data formats you can't interpret.
Disagreement with a buyer after an export is rejected and clarification has been attempted.
An urgent business need that requires faster resolution than a standard rejection/resubmission.

blocks.text: What to Include in Your Escalation:

items: Project code and creation date from the export request.
Screenshot highlighting the specific concern.
What you've already tried.
Why this needs escalation (e.g., "Buyer claims urgent business deadline").

blocks.text: What Buyers See
Understanding what guidance buyers receive helps you provide better feedback:
Buyers are told the following:

items: "Omnisient permits only the download of aggregated results".
They must confirm their export "does not contain information that could lead to the identification of any individual".
Their request will be reviewed by data partners and Omnisient.

blocks.text: What buyers don't automatically see:

items: Specific examples of what qualifies as "aggregated".
The red flags you're checking for (sequential IDs, obfuscation, etc.)

blocks.text: Your rejection feedback is often the first time a buyer learns what's actually required. Ensure your rejection reason is educational:
"This doesn't look aggregated"

"This export contains fields with sequential values (Customer_Type: CUST_10001, CUST_10002...) which appear to be identifiers rather than aggregated categories. Please revise your query to group data into meaningful segments (e.g., customer types: 'Frequent Buyer', 'Occasional', 'New') rather than exporting individual customer records."
Maintaining Consistency Across Your Review Team
If multiple people at your organization review SQLPad exports:
Best Practices

items: Designate a lead reviewer who makes final calls on edge cases.
Review first 5-10 exports together to calibrate standards.
Document your decisions. Keep internal notes on why specific exports were approved/rejected to build institutional knowledge.
Weekly sync (15 min) to discuss any unclear cases and align on standards.
Share this guide with all reviewers and confirm everyone understands the "reject if unsure" principle.

blocks.text: If Reviewers Disagree

items: Default to the MORE CAUTIOUS position: rejection.
Escalate to your lead reviewer or our support team.
Never approve if any reviewer has unresolved concerns.

blocks.text: Building Your Review Library
Consider keeping screenshots of:

items: Good examples you've approved (reference for future).
Bad examples you've rejected (training for new reviewers).
Edge cases you escalated (learn from support's guidance).

blocks.text: Conclusion

Reviewing SQLPad exports doesn’t need to feel complex or intimidating. With a small amount of attention and familiarity, most samples can be assessed quickly and confidently. Paying thoughtful attention to column names, formatting, and overall consistency helps ensure the data aligns with what was intended to be shared.
If something doesn’t immediately make sense, it’s perfectly reasonable to pause, seek clarification, or make use of the Support & Escalation guidance.
By taking a considered approach and using the tools and guidance available, you play an important role in maintaining consistent, well-reviewed data sharing.
Help Us Improve
This guide will evolve based on your feedback.
Have you encountered:

items: An edge case not covered here?
An obfuscation technique we didn't describe?
Unclear guidance that needs improvement?

blocks.text: Share your feedback with us.

chapters.title: Power BI Reports

blocks.text: Power BI: Unveiling the Power of Data Visualization

Power BI is a dynamic ecosystem comprising software services, applications, and connectors, harmoniously engineered to transform disparate data sources into cohesive, visually captivating, and interactive insights. Power BI seamlessly connects to your data sources, enabling you to visualize, explore, and communicate key insights with ease.
Connecting and Visualizing Data
Build visually engaging reports that bring your data to life and help you uncover valuable insights.
Paginated Reports for Operational Insights
Explore another essential workflow in Power BI, focused on paginated reports.
Paginated reports are meticulously designed to fit neatly on a page and are often utilized for operational reporting purposes.
These reports present all data in a tabular format, ensuring comprehensive visibility, even across multiple pages.
Consuming Reports in the Power BI Service
In the Power BI service, you can seamlessly consume and interact with reports, as well as individual visual elements, directly from the Omnisient app.
Gain actionable insights and make informed decisions based on the reports generated within the Power BI environment.

With Power BI, the power of data visualization is at your fingertips. Empower yourself to unlock the full potential of your data, from connecting to diverse data sources to creating compelling reports and paginated insights. Whether you're a data analyst, business user, or decision-maker, Power BI equips you with the tools to drive meaningful outcomes and propel your organization forward. Explore the possibilities with Power BI and revolutionize the way you harness data-driven insights.

chapters.title: Export Power BI Reports as PDF, PNG, or PPT
chapters.part: Analytics tools: SQLPad, Jupyter and Power BI

blocks.text: We’ve introduced a powerful export feature for Power BI reports in the Omnisient platform. This guide explains how to export reports in PDF, PNG, or PPT formats, either as individual pages or as a full report.
Target Audience
This feature is available to all users who have access to view reports on the platform.
How to Export a Power BI Report
Step-by-step Instructions

items: Open a Power BI Report Navigate to the report you want to export.
Click either the Export Full Report Button or Export Page Button Locate the Export button, now visible at the top of your report view.
Choose File Format Select your preferred file format from the dropdown:
PDF
PNG
PPT
You’ll see a confirmation message once your export is queued.
Receive Your Report via Email You’ll receive an email with a download link once your report is ready.

blocks.text: Tips and Best Practices

items: For quicker downloads, export individual pages instead of full reports.

blocks.text: Troubleshooting

items: Didn’t receive an email? Check your spam or junk folder. If it’s not there, try exporting again or contact support.
Button not visible? Ensure you have the correct report access permissions. If issues persist, reach out to your administrator or support support@omnisient.com.

blocks.text: If you have further questions, contact support@omnisient.com or use the Help button in the web app.
